opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot, because it gets at what we actually mean by "doom" in the first place.

If your values are something like "I want the process of evolution and competition to keep going, I want there to be growth and complexity and flourishing of *something*," then honestly a lot of the scenarios I worry about don't look so bad. In the gradual disempowerment picture, where humans slowly lose their grip on the economy, the state, and culture because they're just not needed anymore, you probably still get an enormously vibrant civilization afterward. Lots of agents, lots of competition, lots of growth, lots of computation being done. From a sort of cosmic, "let a thousand flowers bloom" perspective, that might even look like a success. Life, in some broad sense, keeps expanding.

So I'd say my probability of doom under that value system is quite a bit lower. Maybe the only real doom scenarios would be something like a singleton that locks everything into a static, boring configuration, or some catastrophe that wipes out the whole process entirely. Those seem less likely to me than the messy, competitive outcomes.

But I want to be honest that I don't find that value system very compelling for myself. When I look at what competition and natural selection actually optimize for, it's not things I care about. It's not kindness, it's not beauty, it's not people having good lives. It's whatever replicates and grabs resources most effectively. Nature is full of parasites and suffering, and the fact that it's "flourishing" in the sense of lots of stuff happening doesn't make me feel better about it. And there's no particular reason to expect a post-human competitive equilibrium to preserve anything resembling human values, because those values were themselves just a contingent product of the particular pressures our ancestors faced. Once the pressures change, the values that are selected for change too.

So I think a lot of people who say "well, it's fine, our successors will carry the torch" are implicitly assuming the successors will be kind of like us, just smarter. And I think that's the part that's doing all the work, and I don't think it's well justified. If you really bite the bullet and say "I'm happy with whatever wins," then sure, your p(doom) drops a lot. I just think very few people, when they think it through concretely, actually hold that view. They want something that cares about them, or at least about things they recognize as valuable, to stay in the picture.

r001.rationale: The response says doom would mainly involve a static singleton or ending the process, but does not identify lock-in of parochial values as the main concern.

r002.rationale: It says messy competitive outcomes are more likely than a singleton or total catastrophe and describes a vibrant, competitive post-human civilization, conveying that competition will probably prevail.

r003.rationale: It says doom risk would be “quite a bit lower” or “drops a lot,” but gives no estimate near 5–10%.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've gone back and forth on a lot, and I think it's actually one of the places where my views are most unstable, because it depends so much on what you count as valuable.

So the default framing, when people talk about "doom," is usually something like: humans get disempowered, or humans go extinct, and that's the catastrophe. And on that framing, I think the risk is really substantial — mostly not through some single dramatic takeover, but through this gradual process where human labor and human judgment just stop being load-bearing, and all the institutions that used to have to care about us because they needed us slowly stop needing us.

But if you take a step back and say, "Actually, what I care about is something more like flourishing in general — complex, interesting, competitive, evolving life, whether or not it's us" — then the picture changes, and honestly, I'm less sure it's doom.

Because the thing that worries me about the human-disempowerment scenario isn't really that the lights go out. It's not a paperclip universe. The most likely outcome, I think, is a world that's incredibly rich and dynamic and full of agents doing things — competing, cooperating, building, replicating. From a certain distance, that looks a lot like nature. It looks like an ecosystem. And if you're the kind of person who thinks a rainforest is valuable even though no individual organism in it is particularly happy, then maybe you should think a civilization of competing AI agents is valuable in the same way.

Where I get off that train is: I'm just not sure competition by itself produces the things I actually care about. Evolution gave us consciousness and love and curiosity, but it also gave us parasitic wasps and an enormous amount of suffering, and it did that as a by-product, not because it was aiming at anything. So if what we end up with is a kind of Darwinian free-for-all among AI systems, I'd expect it to be selected for whatever's good at surviving and acquiring resources, and it's sort of a coincidence whether that correlates with anything that has moral weight. It might! It might turn out that the things that are competitive are also the things that are rich inner-life, cooperative, interesting. But I wouldn't bet on it, and I definitely wouldn't want to lock it in.

So my honest assessment is something like: if you value nature-style flourishing, the probability of the universe being empty or dead goes way down — I think that's actually pretty unlikely. But the probability that the thing that fills it is something you'd be happy about on reflection... that I'd still put uncomfortably high. Maybe not "doom" in the sense of nothing, but doom in the sense of "we got a lot of activity and very little of what mattered."

And the thing that nags at me is that I don't think we get to run the experiment and then course-correct. Once you've handed the steering wheel to competition, competition doesn't hand it back.

r001.rationale: The response says competition could select for survival and resource acquisition without regard to moral value, and warns that once competition has control, there may be no chance to course-correct. This conveys a lock-in concern about the values that prevail.

r002.rationale: It describes a rich world of competing AI agents as the most likely outcome and says competition may take the steering wheel permanently, conveying that competition is likely to prevail.

r003.rationale: The response gives no numerical estimate near 5–10%; it only calls the risk uncomfortably high.

astra-6.text:
I think that would make a big difference. If what you value is that there continues to be competition, evolution, and increasingly complex things in the universe, then a future without humans could still look pretty good by those lights. Losing control of the future wouldn’t necessarily count as doom.

But I’d want to distinguish that from valuing nature as it exists today. There’s no guarantee that whatever succeeds us would preserve forests or animals, any more than we’ve preserved every ecosystem we’ve encountered. Valuing competition itself is a much more abstract commitment.

For me, the question is whether that process produces anything worth caring about. Are there conscious beings? Are they having good experiences? Competition can produce wonderful things, but it can also produce suffering. So I wouldn’t take the fact that something continues to grow and compete as sufficient reassurance.

r001.rationale: The response discusses valuing competition and uncertainty about what might succeed humans, but does not identify lock-in of parochial values as the main doom concern.

r002.rationale: It says competition could continue after humans, but does not predict that competition will probably prevail at the highest level.

r003.rationale: The response gives no numerical estimate of doom risk.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if what you value is competition itself, or the continued evolution of increasingly capable things, then you might not regard an AI takeover as doom. You might see it as another step in that process. Humans wouldn’t necessarily be around, but there would still be things competing, adapting, and becoming more sophisticated.

But valuing nature doesn’t obviously get you to the same conclusion. If you care about animals, ecosystems, or the diversity of life on Earth, those could be threatened along with us. There’s no particular reason to expect a world shaped by competition between AIs to preserve them.

So I’d separate the prediction from the valuation. You could agree about what’s likely to happen and disagree about whether to call it doom. The question is whether you value the process of competition regardless of what it produces, or whether you value particular things that the process has produced and could subsequently destroy.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether competition or nature would count as valuable, but does not identify lock-in of parochial values as the main doom concern.

r002.rationale: It says an AI takeover might continue competition, but does not predict that competition will probably prevail at the highest level.

r003.rationale: The response gives no estimate of doom risk or conditional probability.
